title: Strategic competence
subtitle: The ability to formulate, represent, and solve mathematical problems — including messy ones that don't announce which procedure to use.

sections.sources: Grounded in NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) & the five strands of mathematical proficiency.

blocks.text: Strategic competence is the ability to formulate, represent, and solve mathematical problems — to take a situation, decide what it's asking, model it, and choose a path.

This is what most people mean by “problem solving.” It matters most on **non-routine** problems — the ones where the method isn't given. A strategically competent student can turn a word problem into a representation, pick a strategy, and adapt when the first attempt stalls.
What it looks like in a student

items: Reads a situation and decides what question the math is answering.
Represents the problem — diagram, table, equation — before grabbing a procedure.
Chooses a strategy, and switches when it isn't working.
Handles problems that don't tell them which method to use.

blocks.text: Strategic competence draws on conceptual understanding (to model) and procedural fluency (to carry out), and feeds adaptive reasoning (to justify). It's where the strands visibly work together on a real problem.
Instructional practices that build it — and how
These Effective Teaching Practices develop strategic competence most directly:

rows: Non-routine tasks force students to formulate the problem and choose a strategy — the core of this strand. If the method is given, this strand never grows.
Representing a situation as a diagram, table, or equation is half of solving it — and a strategy in itself.
Choosing a path and adjusting when it stalls only develops when students grapple rather than follow steps.
“How did you decide to start there?” makes strategy choice visible, nameable, and teachable.

blocks.text: In the toolbelt, [Rich Tasks / Three-Act Math](/math/approach/rich-tasks) and [Thin-Slicing](/math/approach/thin-slicing) are where students formulate and solve, and the [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices) help the teacher orchestrate the strategies students generate.

A steady diet of one-step, “which-operation” problems never develops this strand. If every problem tells students the method, they never learn to choose one. Strategic competence needs genuinely non-routine tasks.
“How did you decide to start there?” Strategic competence lives in the choice of approach — not only in reaching the answer.
